chapter_theme: The six Kalahasti verses hold the body and its life up against the Lord. A life runs from the womb through silk, pearls and play to a corpse mourned by corpses-to-be; gold is useful to its owner but the owner is no use to gold, and so the worshipper is no use to the Lord; the poet cannot match the heroic devotions of the Nayanars and asks how else he can become a servant; and the Lord has arranged his eating, sleeping, lust and deathbed terror, so when will he see him? The last two verses turn on the body of the women he circles: a pit, an oozing wound, a hidden door of lust, from which the petty pleasure must be given up.
structure_note: All six verses end on Kalathi (Kalahasti) and its Lord. 314 and 315 are reflections, 316 and 317 are questions (how shall I become a servant, when shall I see you), and 318 and 319 are pleas to be taken and raised, built on the same image of the woman's body.

314.reading: Having entered the ten and been born and grown, wrapped in silk, decked in pearls and coral, having run and played and come to the end, one lies there a corpse; what is the reckoning of the corpses-to-be who wail beside it? See, Kalathi of Kailasa city.
314.nuance: பத்தும் புகுந்து is taken by tradition as the ten months in the womb; it could also be the ten airs or the ten senses entering the body. சாம்பிணங்கள், 'the corpses that will die', makes the mourners already corpses, so the wailing is one corpse over another.

315.reading: Gold is of use to those who possess it; what use is the possessor to the gold? In the same way, from you I have every use I could want; what use is there to you in me, who bow to you? Lord of Kalathi.
315.nuance: The analogy is exact and cuts against the worshipper: the Lord is the gold and the devotee the owner who gains everything and gives nothing. The verse neither asks for anything nor claims merit; it only states the one-sidedness of the relation, which is its humility.

316.reading: I am not one who can cut up my child with a sword and serve it; I am not one who can give up youth on the word of a woman's oath; I am not one who can serve and, on the sixth day, set my eye into the eye. How then shall I go now and become a servant to the father of Thirukalathi?
316.nuance: The three feats are those of the Nayanars as tradition tells them: Siruthondar who cooked his son for the Lord's guest, Thiruneelakanda who kept a vow of celibacy from youth at his wife's oath, and Kannappar at this very shrine, who on the sixth day of his service plucked out his eye for the bleeding image. The poet does not scorn these; he says he cannot do them, and leaves the question of another way open.

317.reading: You have arranged that I eat rice three times a day and sleep, that in infatuation I join women whose young breasts are like bronze, and that when the life departs my eyes are troubled, Lord. When will I be able to see you? Lord of Thirukalathi.
317.nuance: வைத்தாய், 'you set it so', gives the whole ordinary life, including lust and the terror of dying, to the Lord's arrangement; the complaint is that he arranged everything but the seeing. Read with 304 and 350, the surrender of agency is the poet's constant stance, here turned into a reproach.

318.reading: Wandering night and day for prey and growing weary here, circling the pit of misery at women's waists, the oozing hollow where fluid seeps, I am a lone one who goes round and round; take me and rule me, Kalathi who sits in grace under the stone banyan on the bank of the golden Mugali.
318.nuance: இரைக்கே, for prey or for food, makes the man an animal foraging; the woman's body is a pit (குழி) and a seeping hollow (புரை). கல்லால நிழல், the shade of the stone banyan, is the seat of Siva as Dakshinamurti, the silent teacher, set against the poet's restless circling.

319.reading: The reeking stream like a horse's water, the hole in the skin where pus seeps daily, the pit of filth, the doorway of lust, the hidden wound, the cleft of flesh within the inner chamber: grant me the state of rising, having left the petty pleasure that lies there, Lord of Thirukalathi.
319.nuance: The whole verse is one description of the woman's sex, in the register of disgust the Naladiyar uses for the body. சிற்றின்பம், the small pleasure, is the standard counter to பேரின்பம், the great bliss of 353; ஏறும் பதம், the rising state, is the ascent out of it. The verse asks the Lord to grant the leaving, not for strength to leave.

links.note: Both watch the mourners rather than the dead: Tirumular's town wails, burns the body, bathes and stops thinking of him; Pattinathar's mourners are themselves corpses-to-be (சாம்பிணங்கள்) wailing beside a corpse. Tirumular shows that grief ends; Pattinathar that the grievers end.

316 confesses that the poet cannot do what Siruthondar, Thiruneelakanda and Kannappar did and asks how else to become a servant. Tirumular's verse answers the question: even making one's bones firewood and frying one's flesh does not reach the gem; only those who melt with love do. Pattinathar's own answer comes at 324, in melting and tears.

Both describe the desired body as a vessel of filth: the Naladiyar's pot that seeps from nine openings and churns with slime, dazzling the fool with its dark skin; Pattinathar's pus-hole, pit of filth and hidden wound. The Naladiyar blames the fool's eye; Pattinathar asks for the state that leaves the pleasure behind.

Tirumular reproaches the dull who call the body filth (மலம் என்று உடம்பை மதியாத) and hold some other place sacred, since the whole cosmos is grasped in the strong body. Pattinathar calls the body a filth-pit and a hidden wound and asks to rise out of it. On the reading that Tirumular means the human body as such, and not only the yogi's, the two value the body oppositely; Pattinathar's verse is about the woman's body as an object of lust, which narrows but does not remove the conflict.

Both poets describe themselves as foragers: Pattinathar wanders night and day for prey (இரைக்கே) round the pit at women's waists; Arunagirinathar carries a body that stinks like a corpse from house to house, speaking sweetly for whatever feast comes. Each asks the Lord to end the circuit, Pattinathar by being taken and ruled, Arunagirinathar by bowing at the feet.
